title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

AbstractTools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization.

MainProgrammable small RNA–protein complexes such as CRISPR–Cas enable a single protein to serve as a flexible scaffold for diverse manipulations of nucleic acids. Small RNAs used as guides are stabilized by binding to their protein partner, offer unparalleled ease of target programming and can be chemically modified to improve their properties1. The sequence-specific manipulation of RNA by RNA-guided effectors has emerged as a ubiquitous mechanism for RNA regulation in prokaryotes and eukaryotes2,3. Cas13/type VI CRISPR systems and, more broadly, OMEGA-family proteins derived from prokaryotes have been imported into mammalian cells to generate programmable RNA-modulating proteins4,5,6. Catalytically active Cas13 proteins perform targeted RNA cleavage7, while nuclease-deactivated dCas13 proteins can be fused to deaminase enzymes to edit RNA sequences5,8. Fusion of dCas13 to different effectors enables systems that alter9 and sense10 post-transcriptional modifications, such as nucleobase methylation, and modulate mRNA splicing or translation11,12,13. In all cases, Cas13 serves as a short guide RNA (gRNA)-programmed domain that binds RNA targets to induce proximity to an effector domain, uniting sequence-specific targeting with functional modules.Despite their flexibility in function, these systems are limited by off-target activity, unknown interactions with regulatory machinery and the large size of Cas13 (refs. 14,15,16). Although genome mining17,18 and protein engineering19,20 continue to produce smaller variants, therapeutic applications of Cas-derived complexes encounter challenges with immunogenicity and delivery21,22,23. These challenges are compounded when targeting RNA because of the potential requirement for repeat dosing because of RNA turnover. As evidenced by Cas proteins, most biotechnologies for manipulating mammalian cells in a programmable fashion use some nonnative components, potentially creating homeostatic and immunogenic liabilities while sacrificing the evolutionary optimization of mammalian proteins. In contrast, reprogramming mammalian machinery to perform targeted RNA manipulations may be advantageous for biotechnological and therapeutic applications.Programmable RNA effectors with improved immune tolerance and size have been designed in a bottom-up fashion from pieces of mammalian proteins and oligo-RNAs24. Similar to Cas proteins, the interactions of these assemblies with the cellular environment and the immune system remain unknown. Removal of the components from their evolutionary context could remove advantageous properties and interactions while simultaneously disrupting those of the endogenous donor protein. As an alternative concept, identifying exogenous reprogramming agents that induce a range of functions by hijacking existing pathways could enable conservation of evolutionarily optimized properties while retaining benefits of compatibility with the host system. Mammalian cells have the ability to use small RNAs to program the Argonaute (AGO) family of proteins to downregulate a matching target2. A detailed understanding of the RNA interference (RNAi) pathway has enabled engineered small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapies that guide AGO2 to degrade a target transcript25. In principle, human AGO proteins and their native interactors already exhibit many of the advantageous properties of Cas proteins without the need to build a chassis to accomplish target and gRNA recognition. AGO2–gRNA complexes can efficiently sample cellular RNAs for targets26,27 and show enhanced binding kinetics and affinity compared to both Cas13 (refs. 28,29,30) and free RNA base pairing26,27. Despite the advances in harnessing AGO2 for downregulation-based therapeutics and unbiased screening of the transcriptome31, the intrinsic functions of AGO2 are limited. Here, we describe reprogramming of human AGO2 with guides designed to selectively enable the activity of a fused effector on an RNA target. Specifically, we develop a C-to-U RNA base editor termed AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER), which accesses dCas-like function from a human, small RNA-programmable scaffold.Loop-inducing gRNAs enable RNA editing by AGO2–APOBEC3A (A3A) fusionsExtensive biological, structural and biochemical studies of AGO2 activity have elucidated gRNA parameters that lead to optimal downregulation28,29. Consequently, these observations provide a map to program AGO2 for nondegradative binding. Ideal targeting, nondegradative small RNA guides would fail to induce target cleavage and downregulation while retaining useful, evolutionarily optimized properties of RNA-loaded AGO2 such as dramatically increased rates of target binding, high and tunable target affinity26,28,29, the ability to bind despite target secondary structure32 and cellular regulation that promotes efficient target turnover to boost catalytic activity33,34.The anatomy of siRNAs can be divided into five distinct segments with different effects on target binding and cleavage (Fig. 1a). The 5′ base (g1) is anchored in a pocket of AGO2 (ref. 35). Complementarity is critical to target binding in the seed region (g2–g8) and increases affinity for the target in the supplementary region (g13–g16). Full complementarity in the central region (g9–g12) marginally reduces target affinity but is required for target cleavage. Lastly, base pairing in the tail region (g17 to the end of the siRNA) is largely inconsequential to target binding. Therefore, small RNAs with central region mismatches can be used to impart high-affinity binding to a complementary target without inducing target cleavage28,29. The majority of human microRNAs (miRNAs) use this binding mode to recruit repressive factors instead of slicing their targets36. However, most miRNAs target the 3′ untranslated region (UTR), sometimes with multiple binding sites, to effectively mediate downregulation37. Small RNA guides with strategic mismatches designed to target unique or non-3′UTR sites in a target transcript could allow AGO2 binding without potent downregulation. With these parameters, we sought to convert AGO2 to a platform for RNA manipulation.Fig. 1: ALTER design and guide optimization.Full size imagea, The functional regions of siRNA and the impact of guide–target base pairing on target affinity and cleavage within each region. b, Schematic of ALTER editing. Data points indicate replicates; bar heights indicate means. g1–g21, gRNA bases 1–21, counting from the 5′ end; nt, nontargeting guide; tgt, targeting guide; Dox, doxycycline.Source dataAPOBEC proteins are known to act on single-stranded RNAs (ssRNAs) to catalyze a deamination reaction that results in C-to-U sequence editing38,39. A3A selectively edits native substrates that position the target C in the 3′ portion of stem loops40. We envisioned that if AGO2 were fused to A3A, a central mismatch in the gRNA could be used to induce an ssRNA loop around a target position, creating a favorable editing substrate without downregulating the target transcript (Fig. 1b). The feasibility of this design was supported by modeling in AlphaFold3 (ref. 41), which showed correct folding of the protein fusion components and association of A3A with the unbound portion of the RNA target (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1a). Previously developed C-to-U RNA base editors show potential to correct pathogenic T-to-C mutations42 but have not been applied therapeutically, likely as a function of immunogenicity and efficacy5,8.We considered three parameters in gRNA design that could dictate the conformation of the ALTER ternary complex: (1) the size of the induced ssRNA loop (x); (2) the position of the target C within that loop (y); and (3) loop orientation with respect to the gRNA (i, j) (Fig. 1b). We used EGFPY66H (ref. 43), a weakly blue fluorescent mutant of EGFP that is rescued by a C-to-U edit (Fig. 1d), as a reporter. We engineered HEK293T cells to constitutively express EGFPY66H to limit variation in reporter levels between experiments. Our initial protein construct consisted of wild-type (wt) AGO2 fused to A3AY132D (ALTER-1)44. Transfection of the reporter cells with ALTER-1 and gRNA 14L8(11,10), which induces a 14-nt ssRNA loop between g11 and g12 that places the target C at position 8 (ref. 8), induced significant fluorescence (Fig. 1d). Usage of a nontargeting guide, expression of A3A alone or exclusion of the guide, AGO2, A3A or the peptide linker in ALTER-1 did not lead to similar levels of fluorescence. These experiments support the proposed mechanism where ALTER-1 binds a target in a guide sequence-defined manner and induces editing. To assess knockdown caused by the 14L8(11,10) guide, we integrated destabilized GFP (ddGFP)45 into HEK293T cells and transfected nontargeting, fully complementary and 14L8(11,10) shRNAs. The 14L8(11,10) guide did not reduce ddGFP fluorescence compared to the nontargeting control, demonstrating a lack of activity stemming from endogenous AGO2 (Extended Data Fig. 1b). Overexpression of ALTER-1 with the 14L8(11,10) guide (abbreviated 14L8) led to a marginal decrease in fluorescence compared to the guide alone but no significant change compared to ALTER-1 overexpression with a nontargeting guide. These results support that loop-inducing guides lead to minimal AGO2-mediated knockdown of the target.To further probe the highlighted gRNA design parameters, we designed additional 21-nt guides. Guides that altered the loop size (x) while keeping the relative position of the target base consistent (that is, the relative distance from the 5′ and 3′ loop ends) showed that smaller loops led to an apparent lack of editing, while expansion of the loop size to 20 nt reduced editing efficiency (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 1c). Shifting placement of the target C (y) within a 14-nt loop showed similar editing when the target was at position 6, 7 or 8. Conversely, placing the target at position 9 or 10 led to pronounced decreases in fluorescence, potentially a result of steric shielding of the target from A3A by AGO2 (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1d). Lastly, varying the position of the loop with respect to the gRNA (i, j) showed that shifting the loop toward the 5′ end of the gRNA, which disrupts complementarity in its seed region, reduced editing while shifting to the 3′ end led to a less pronounced decrease (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 1e). This overall binding mode, where all bases of the gRNA are complementary to the target but not contiguously, is atypical for native miRNAs. To examine canonical miRNA binding modes, we designed guides with one or three mismatches in the central region, both of which decreased editing activity (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Together, these data demonstrate that a novel, loop-inducing binding mode for gRNAs inside of AGO2 generates favorable substrates for A3A enzymes. Editing guides can be effectively delivered as both plasmid-encoded shRNAs and exogenous siRNA duplexes (Fig. 1h).ALTER activity can be improved by rational protein engineeringModifications that ablate nuclease activity2, reduce noncleaving target downregulation46 or minimize the size of the protein through domain truncation47 could be beneficial to AGO2 neofunction induction (Fig. 2a). AGO2 has been extensively characterized through mutational studies that perturb its RNAi-related functions. While loop-inducing guides bypass proposed requirements for target cleavage, residual slicing of target transcripts could impact ALTER editing efficiency. To first test whether complete removal of nuclease activity would lead to greater editing signal, we investigated whether the use of AGO isoforms, AGO1 and AGO3, which do not cleave targets with standard-length shRNAs, would improve ALTER48,49. While ALTER constructs using these isoforms led to guide-dependent editing, the resulting signal was significantly lower than ALTER-1 (Extended Data Fig. 2a), possibly because lack of nuclease activity can impact efficiency of guide loading25 or because of differences in guide structure preferences between AGO2 and AGO1/3 (refs. 49). Second, we manipulated AGO2 nuclease activity with several reported amino acid substitutions (Fig. 2b). D597A and D669A led to decreased editing activity while H634P did not significantly differ in activity from ALTER-1. Conversely, the Q633R substitution led to a pronounced increase in ALTER activity. This substitution has been reported to ablate slicing only in certain cases2,49 but may also increase ALTER activity by increasing electrostatic affinity to the negatively charged target RNA. Changes in AGO2’s charge are a known mechanism for regulating its affinity for target mRNAs33,34. AGO2 mutants that ablated GW182-binding to prevent miRNA-mediated target downregulation did not appreciably change ALTER activity, supporting that ALTER binding does not downregulate the target transcript by this mechanism (Supplementary Fig. 3)50. The double mutant AGO2F470V;F505V, located in the AGO2 MID domain (Fig. 2c, left), has been shown to reduce nonslicing downregulation of the target RNA, although the underlying mechanism remains unclear46,51,52,53,54. Incorporating this substitution into ALTER resulted in a modest decrease in signal but a more dramatic decrease in background signal from the editor with a nontargeting guide, potentially through decreased association with P-bodies (Fig. 2c, right). Proximity to mRNAs in P-bodies might lead to increases in background and signal, which are both removed by AGO2F470V;F505V. NS, not significant.Source dataSmaller constructs can benefit delivery with state-of-the-art vectors such as AAVs, which has led to numerous efforts toward Cas miniaturization through genome mining17,18 or truncation19,20. We reasoned that thorough characterization of AGO2 activity in RNAi studies might enable rational truncation of AGO2. Removal of the 127-aa PAZ domain of AGO2 (Fig. 2d, left) has been shown to reduce target cleavage and downregulation while maintaining the ability to load small RNAs and bind target transcripts47. Incorporating AGO2∆PAZ into an ALTER editor led to a twofold increase in signal from edited EGFPY66H and a simultaneous decrease in background signal with the nontargeting guide (Fig. 2d, right). Modeling of AGO2∆PAZ with AlphaFold3 (ref. 41) supported minimal impact on the structure of the other AGO2 domains (Fig. 2d, left).In combination, some AGO2 modifications showed additive effects (Fig. 2e). When compared by fusion to A3AY132D, the triple-mutant AGO2F470V;F505V;Q633R led to a small increase in editing activity and a significant drop in background activity compared with wtAGO2. AGO2∆PAZ;Q633R led to both significantly increased signal and decreased background. Conversely, all AGO2 mutants with both the ∆PAZ modification and the F470V;F505V double mutant did not have detectable editing activity (Extended Data Fig. 2b).Further efforts to enhance on-target editing activity were conducted by mutating the A3A portion of ALTER. Mutations of A3A impacting the residues that interact with the nucleic acid substrate have been shown to modulate activity and selectivity for RNA over DNA. ALTER-1 used human A3AY132D, reported to limit off-target activity in both DNA and RNA Cas base editors8,44. Use of wtA3A in ALTER led to a modest increase in editing signal without increased background as gauged with the nontargeting guide. We also tested A3A substitutions known to have increased activity on RNA and negligible activity on DNA (Fig. 2f)55. While both led to increased background activity, the A3AK30R;Y132D mutant also led to a significant increase in targeted editing.Having identified substitutions in both proteins of ALTER able to modulate on-target and background activity, we investigated simultaneous mutations of both domains in single editors (Fig. 2g). AGO2F470V;F505V;Q633R–A3AY132D (ALTER-2) showed minimal signal with the nontargeting guide and higher on-target activity than ALTER-1. ALTER-3, AGO2∆PAZ;Q633R–wtA3A, also showed decreased background with higher editing activity than ALTER-2. Usage of A3AK30R;Y132D instead of wtA3A in ALTER-3 greatly reduced its activity and caused a pronounced increase in background signal (Supplementary Fig. 23). Lastly, AGO2F470V;F505V;Q633R–A3AK30R;Y132G produced lower background activity than ALTER-3 with a nearly twofold increase in editing, resulting in the optimized editor ALTER-4.Human A3A is limited by strict selectivity for UC sequence context and we investigated whether we could expand the range of editable contexts within the ALTER framework. Other human APOBECs have different selectivity; for example, A1 requires an AC context for deamination39. However, incorporation of A1 into ALTER did not result in editing of a recoded EGFPY66H reporter (Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Alternatively, sequence specificity can also be achieved in APOBEC hybrids by grafting together domains from different isoforms. Incorporating the deaminase domain of A1 into A3A (A3AddA1) has been shown to produce an active GC deaminase56, which we used in AGO2F470V;F505V;Q633R–A3AddA1 (ALTER-5). ALTER-5 showed efficient editing in a GC variant of the EGFPY66H reporter and significant activity with an AC reporter (Fig. 2h; note that fluorescence signals result from different cell lines bearing the different recoded EGFPY66H variants). While ALTER-5 demonstrates that different effector domains can be fused to AGO2 to change function, we conducted further characterization with ALTER-4 because of its high activity and selectivity for UC targets and human components that would minimize immunogenicity.To further probe the interaction of guide design and protein construct, additional gRNA designs were tested across ALTER-1–ALTER-4. These designs can be categorized as (1) guides with mismatches in the 3′ region that could potentially retain binding affinity and circumvent target-directed miRNA degradation (TDMD; Extended Data Fig. 2e–h)57,58 or (2) guides that varied the loop size while holding either the 5′ or 3′ portion of 14L8 consistent (Extended Data Fig. 2i–l). These experiments revealed three guides that conveyed higher editing activity with ALTER-1. Specifically, 14L8 with mismatches at g12 and g13 (14L8(12–13 mm)), a guide with the same 5′ region as 14L8 that induced a smaller loop (12L6) and a guide with the same 3′ region that induced a larger loop (18L12) all led to a ~2.5-fold increase in activity in the EGFPY66H editing assay. Additional mismatches in the 3′ region of the guide that may attenuate TDMD removed editing efficacy; thus, the impact of TDMD on ALTER efficacy was not apparent. Guide activity trends were inconsistent with ALTER-3 and ALTER-4. For ALTER-3, all three of the guides that increased activity with ALTER-1 were less effective than 14L8. For ALTER-4, 18L12 was less effective, and 14L8(12–13 mm) and 12L6 were more effective but by a reduced margin compared to ALTER-1 (Extended Data Fig. 2m,n). Together, these data establish a prospective set of initial test guide designs for editing experiments that could lead to enhanced activity.ALTER is a highly active editor of endogenous RNA targetsThe two classes of Cas-fusion C-to-U RNA base editors are typified by RNA editing for specific C-to-U exchange (RESCUE)59 and C-to-U RNA editor (CURE)8. RESCUE consists of dRanCas13b fused to an engineered adenosine deaminase acting on RNA (ADAR) variant that can deaminate both cytidine and adenosine (Fig. 3a, right), whereas CURE is a dPspCas13b–A3AY132D fusion (Fig. 3a, left). We directly compared the editing abilities of ALTER, RESCUE-S and CURE-N in HEK293T-EGFPY66H cells. CURE-N showed minimal fluorescence signal, while RESCUE-S was threefold less active than ALTER-4 (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 3a). We confirmed editing of transcripts by sequencing (Fig. 3c) and qPCR confirmed that no editor led to significant EGFPY66H transcript knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 3b). These data revealed a linear relationship between rescued fluorescence of the EGFPY66H cells and C-to-U editing percentage quantified by sequencing analysis (Extended Data Fig. 3c–f). Target positions by gene, transcript and location: PPIB ENST00000300026 C90 (UC), SMARCA4 ENST00000647230 C503, ACTB ENST00000646664 C309, TYMS ENST00000323274 C876, MALAT1 ENST00000534336 C1053 and PPIB ENST00000300026 C92 (GC).Source dataWe next assessed the target scope of ALTER on a panel of endogenous transcripts with corresponding 14L8 guides. In previous studies, PPIB C90 was shown to be more effectively edited by CURE-N than RESCUE-S8,59. We also observed this trend and found that ALTER-4 showed the highest level of editing (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). SMARCA4 C503 was more effectively edited by RESCUE-S than CURE-N8,59, with ALTER-4 showing comparable editing to RESCUE-S (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). This suggests that the activity and selectivity of fusion protein editors are likely not solely determined by their effector domains. We also used ALTER-4 to edit ACTB C309 and TYMS C876, two other sites that RESCUE and CURE have been shown to edit effectively8,59. In both cases, ALTER-4 led to significantly higher levels of C-to-U editing than either Cas-based editor (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 4e–h). For all endogenous targets, we also assessed whether ALTER-4 led to knockdown of the targeted transcript and found any reductions in transcript level to be similar to those caused by the dCas editors (Fig. 3e).Reduced transcript abundance has been reported with dCas13-based constructs previously60 and this depletion effect may reflect a general consequence of nonnative interactions between a transcript and an ectopically expressed protein. In addition to 14L8, we tested 14L8(12–13 mm) and 12L6 guides for ALTER-4 editing of TYMS and PPIB (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Contrary to the activity of similar guides on EGFPY66H, 14L8(12–13 mm) led to comparable PPIB editing to 14L8 while 12L6 decreased activity, whereas the inverse was true for TYMS (Extended Data Figs. 2m,n and 5b). These discrepancies in the performance of guide designs between different targets suggest that optimal guides depend on both the target and editor. In total, ALTER-4 showed comparable or higher activity compared to the Cas editors across a panel of endogenous targets without enhanced target knockdown.To assess whether ALTER could access nuclear transcripts, we targeted the nuclear lncRNA MALAT1. Initial experiments with ALTER-4 showed minimal editing at MALAT1 C1053, suggesting that ALTER may be largely excluded from the nucleus. However, addition of a nuclear localization sequence to the N terminus of ALTER-4 (ALTER-4N) led to a pronounced increase in MALAT1 editing without target knockdown (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 4i–j). While activity remained lower than CURE-N8, which has been engineered with both viral nuclear localization sequences and nuclear export sequences, it may be possible to further optimize for nuclear localization or shuttling. ALTER-4N did not exhibit differences in editing activity of EGFPY66H compared to ALTER-4 (Extended Data Fig. 3g).We also examined whether ALTER-5 could edit endogenous GC targets. We tested editing at PPIB C92 (which is preceded by G)59 and found the editing level to be significantly higher than RESCUE-S and that both editors had similar effects on transcript abundance (Fig. 3g). No CURE variant has been shown to have editing activity in sequence contexts other than UC8.Examining C-to-U changes across the sequencing amplicons for each target revealed two types of potential bystander edits within a target transcript: (1) distal sites that are already primed for A3A editing but may incur further editing with induced proximity (for example, EGFPY66H position 56; Extended Data Fig. 3h,i) or (2) sites in or proximal to the ALTER-induced loop (for example, TYMS position −5; Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). When TYMS was edited with a 12L6 guide (Extended Data Fig. 5a), we observed comparable editing at TYMS C876 to that observed with the 14L8 guide and dramatically reduced bystander editing at C871 (Extended Data Fig. 5d,e). Therefore, guide design can be used to both optimize on-target editing and minimize bystander editing.Assessment of transcriptome-wide off-target activityAs AGO2 is a native human protein and the core scaffold of ALTER, off-target C-to-U editing and differential expression effects could potentially result from both unintended guide interactions and perturbations of endogenous RNAi61. To quantify transcriptome-wide editing activity, we compared mRNA-seq data from cells treated with PPIB-targeted or TYMS-targeted ALTER-4 to a NanoLuc transfection control. Targeting PPIB, we observed only 518 high-confidence off-target edits, which was fourfold lower than the corresponding numbers reported for RESCUE-S and CURE-N8. TYMS-targeted ALTER-4 led to a higher number of off-targets, indicating that the magnitude of off-target editing may be highly guide and target dependent (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6a–c). Lowering the amount of transfected ALTER-4 resulted in a clear dose response in TYMS editing (Extended Data Fig. 5g–h). Notably, treating cells with a reduced dose of ALTER-4, which provides comparable TYMS editing to a full dose of CURE-N or RESCUE-S (Extended Data Fig. 5i), led to a 25-fold drop in the number of off-target edits (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6a–c). This experiment demonstrates that, even when using a guide prone to increased off-target editing, when normalized to target editing efficiency, ALTER can result in substantially reduced off-targets. We mapped each off-target edit site (position 0) to corresponding expressed transcripts and analyzed their RNA contexts. There is a clear consensus sequence from −4 to +1 and preference for stem-loop secondary structures62, matching previously described characteristics of A3A editing hotspots (Fig. 4b–d and Extended Data Fig. 6d–e)63. This result suggests that ALTER-4 off-targets predominantly arise from collateral A3A activity, which is further supported by our finding that 73% of ALTER-4 off-target edits also appear when A3A is overexpressed, alone or as a component of a CURE editor (Extended Data Fig. 6f–h).Fig. 4: Quantification of transcriptome-wide effects of ALTER.Full size imagea, Quantified off-targets identified in RNA-seq data from HEK293T cells transfected with plasmids encoding each editor.
